cards.title: Offer vs discount: the five levers of an ecommerce offer
cards.summary: An offer has five components — product positioning, price architecture, value mechanic, risk reversal and urgency — and discount only occupies the price-architecture slot.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing whether a store has an ad problem, an offer problem or a discounting problem before investing in new creative, a new PDP or a new site build.
steps: Treat an offer as five components: (1) product positioning — what problem this solves for whom and why now; (2) price architecture — percentage off, threshold offer, UPT structure, bundle; (3) value mechanic — free shipping, free gift, BOGO, samples, second-order tier, subscription unlock; (4) risk reversal — returns, guarantee, trial, sample-only purchase; (5) urgency — drop, seasonality, stock window.
Recognise that a discount only fills the price-architecture slot. The other four levers can carry the offer alone, so a store does not have to discount to have a distinct offer.

Use the perceived-value mechanic deliberately: buyers judge an offer by the gap between what they think the product costs the business and what they receive, so 50–60% off feels like arbitrage even when the brand is profitable. The business goal is the inverse — capture as much spend above COGS as possible while the buyer believes they are paying near cost.
Look for offers genuinely good for both sides: a brand owning software can bundle free licensing at near-zero delivery cost while the consumer sees real savings.
Keep ad, landing page, checkout and email congruent on the same offer, and remove expired promotions from every surface.
caveats: Rotating a new weekly promo across a 52-week calendar trains customers to wait for discounts; the source treats that as a mistake, not a strategy.
Heavy flat discounting permanently re-anchors perceived price, compressing margin structurally rather than just during the promo window.

cards.title: Hierarchy of influences on DTC performance
cards.summary: Budget and account structure are the lowest-leverage levers; creative, offer, brand and product drive the largest performance deltas.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest scarce time when store performance is flat and the team defaults to reshuffling ad budgets and campaign structure.
steps: Rank the levers from least to most powerful for creating a purchase decision: budget (fuel — more spend sells more, but only if everything else works), account structure (can retarget the same people or push the wrong products), creative (how people hear about you), offer (what they get and why now), brand (why they buy from you rather than a competitor), product (why they buy at all, dominant at bottom-funnel and repeat purchase).
Note the trade-off: higher levers create bigger deltas but are harder and slower to change, which is exactly why teams keep fiddling with budget and structure instead.
When a brand believes it has an ad problem, check the offer first; when it believes it has an offer problem, check whether habitual discounting is the real cause.
Treat budget and account structure as prerequisites to fix, not as the place to hunt for an inflection.
caveats: Attributed framework from the presenter; the ranking is his opinion about where leverage sits, not a measured law.
A strong brand or product does not excuse broken account structure — the lower levers can still sink an otherwise strong offer.

cards.title: Model a discount's true economics before running it
cards.summary: Waterfall price, UPT, COGS, gross margin, break-even ROAS and target CPA to see the efficiency a discount actually demands.
cards.use_when: Pressure-testing a proposed percentage-off sale or any price-architecture change against profit rather than top-line revenue.
steps: Baseline the full-price unit: at $100 AOV and $40 all-in COGS (including shipping, fulfilment and transaction fees), gross margin is $60 (60%), break-even ROAS = 1 / 0.60 = 1.67, and at 6x target ROAS the target CPA = 100 / 6 = $16.67, leaving $43.33 contribution profit per order. Do this for every product.
Model the discount per unit, not per order: a 25% discount drops price per unit to $75.
Account for UPT rising during sales — in the worked example UPT went from 1.0 to 1.63, so AOV actually rose to about $122.
Compute COGS against the pre-discount retail value, not the discounted AOV: $162 retail × 40% = $65 COGS, leaving $57 gross margin (22% lower than baseline).
Recalculate: break-even ROAS rises to 2.22, and holding the same contribution profit requires a CAC of about $13.67 (roughly 8.97x ROAS) — about a 50% efficiency improvement over the 6x baseline.

Ask whether that efficiency lift is realistic before launching. The source has seen luxury brands that never discount model 70–80% efficiency lifts, and saturated always-discounting brands model only about 5%.
caveats: The example assumes COGS covers all variable costs and is a simplified illustration, not a benchmark.
Efficiency lift during a sale is brand-specific; it depends on how rarely the brand discounts and how saturated the market already is with its discounting.

cards.title: Build an evergreen offer stack that lowers required efficiency
cards.summary: Layering a 90-day supply, subscription-locked lifetime discount, app access and a mystery gift cut required ROAS from 6x to 2.9x in the worked example.
cards.use_when: Designing a non-discount-led acquisition offer a store can run year-round instead of rotating promos.
steps: Stack components rather than discounting: buy a 90-day supply, get 25% off; free app access with daily meal plans; a free mystery gift; and a 25% discount for life while the customer stays on subscription (double the usual 10%).
Tie the offer to a required action — the buyer only gets the deal if they tick the subscription box — and put urgency behind the lifetime rate.

Model the margin: COGS at 40% of the $253 retail value is $101, but multi-unit shipping costs less than the unit cost baked into price ($36 charged vs $17 actual for three units), pulling true delivery cost to about $82 and gross margin to $108.
Compare to the full-price baseline: holding the same contribution profit per order needs a CAC of about $65, so 190 / 65 ≈ 2.9x ROAS instead of 6x.
Keep the mystery gift out of the COGS model if it is $0–3 (sample packs, cheap drink bottles on large POs, or another brand's product supplied for co-marketing).

Note the retention upside: subscription-locked offers should drive materially more repeat purchase, which can justify more aggressive acquisition spend — the source suggests roughly double the repeat purchasing versus a plain discount, though that is his expectation, not a guarantee.
caveats: The claim that this offer doubles repeat purchase is the presenter's projection for that hypothetical brand, not a measured result.
Do not stack value indefinitely — the source warns that 'simple scales' when it comes to offers.

cards.title: Audit and iterate an offer after 90–120 days live
cards.summary: Survey customers on which offer components actually drove purchase, then cut or fix components that add complexity or damage retention.
cards.use_when: After an evergreen or heavily stacked offer has run a full quarter and you need evidence on what to keep.
steps: Let the offer run 90–120 days before judging its components.
Survey buyers to establish which additions — mystery gift, app access, discount tier — convinced them to purchase.
Remove components nobody cares about and test whether conversion changes without them; the source's example was a mystery gift that may have had zero persuasive value.

Investigate back-end effects of front-end winners: if an app or bonus drove acquisition but customers found it useless, it can lower brand perception and hurt retention revenue, so change the deliverable or remove it.
Iterate on this cycle to raise first-purchase profit, lower CAC and improve retention simultaneously, rather than treating acquisition and retention as separate problems.
caveats: Survey responses are self-reported and may not perfectly predict behaviour without an A/B test.
Removing a component can be tested, but the source does not specify a required sample size or test duration.

cards.title: Discount rate versus contribution profit: small discounts can lose money
cards.summary: Plotting contribution profit against discount rate shows small discounts often subtract margin with no UPT uplift, and required target ROAS rises exponentially near the profit-maximising point.
cards.use_when: Choosing the headline discount percentage for a sale, or deciding whether a discount is viable at all.
steps: Graph discount rate (x-axis) against contribution profit per order (y-axis) using your own historical flat-discount periods.
Expect a decline at low discounts: 5–10% is not convincing enough to lift UPT, so unit price compresses with no offset and contribution profit falls.
Find the inflection where customers begin to care and UPT rises; contribution profit is a function of both average unit retail (falling with discount) and UPT (rising with it).
Locate the discount rate that maximises contribution profit per order — for the source's illustrated brand that was 20% — and headline that percentage rather than defaulting to 25% or more.

Separately model required target ROAS: it rises exponentially as discounting increases because margin compresses toward your profit target much faster than toward zero. The worked illustration put something like a 15% discount at roughly 8x required ROAS and a 25% discount at roughly 20x, which can make deep discounting outright inapplicable.
Keep UPT and efficiency data from past promos consistent enough to make this modelling possible; messy historical discounting makes it unreliable.
caveats: Both break-even and target ROAS curves need your own UPT history; generic benchmarks will mislead.
Past roughly 30–40% discounting the source considers the offer generally not worth it regardless of UPT uplift.

cards.title: Product repositioning: turn one SKU into many offers
cards.summary: Reposition one hero SKU into multiple personas, problems and mechanisms to unlock offers you could not otherwise build.
cards.use_when: You have a single hero SKU or narrow range and cannot construct bundles, thresholds or persona-specific offers.
steps: List the distinct personas, problems and mechanisms the same product can serve. The source's example is a daily greens gummy repositioned into gut health for bloating, GLP1 support, fibre for digestion, hair health, cognition and focus, and a business-professional multivitamin — with many more tested in the account.
Build dedicated landing pages and offers around only the highest-performing angles, tailoring product title and positioning to each while leaving the SKU unchanged.
Attach costless partner value where it fits: for a GLP1-support angle, partner with a GLP1 provider for 25% off, or ask for a clip on future purchases so the offer can be revenue-positive.

Use clinical timelines as offer structure: if hair-health results are only measurable after 90–120 days, headline that requirement and add a free extra 30 days — delivered as one discounted unit on the second 90-day billing rather than extra units in the first order — to preserve first-order margin.
Note that the contribution-margin impact of repositioning is nil or positive, and it works best applied to one hero SKU.
caveats: Persona repositioning can raise regulatory or compliance risk depending on claims and category — the source flags his GLP1 and hair-health examples as ideas, not approved copy.
Without repositioning, most offers collapse into broad generic promotions that fail to cut through to a specific audience.

cards.title: Bundle mechanics: protect margin and promote cheaper
cards.summary: Bundles raise UPT and create shipping/fulfilment economies of scale while protecting contribution margin if the economics are modelled.
cards.use_when: You sell multiple SKUs or a consumable you can package multiple times and want a discount-shaped offer without margin erosion.
steps: Know what a bundle changes: UPT rises necessarily, COGS efficiency comes from shipping and fulfilment rather than unit cost, and contribution margin should improve if the bundle is structured correctly.
Use it for multi-SKU brands, or for consumables where the same SKU can be sold repeatedly — the source's example is buy two board games and get 25% off.
In the worked 90-day example, bundling cut true delivery cost from the $36 baked into price to $17, showing where the scale gain comes from.
Treat bundles as the simple, familiar offer they are: they protect contribution margin, but the source considers them the least creative option and says teams can do much more with the same margin.
caveats: Single-SKU, non-consumable brands cannot use this mechanic.
The source notes interviews asking candidates to define a good offer usually return 'high discount' or 'bundle', implying bundles are the obvious answer rather than a sophisticated one.

cards.title: Gift-with-purchase: nearly double contribution margin at lower break-even ROAS
cards.summary: A low-cost gift that forces a second unit can double contribution margin while slightly lowering the required break-even ROAS.
cards.use_when: You have a cheap secondary SKU or accessory that pairs naturally and want to push UPT without discounting price.
steps: Model the base case (one $50 beach towel, $15 COGS, $8.50 shipping/3PL) at $26.50 contribution margin and a 1.89 break-even ROAS.

Model the offer (buy two for $100, free $4 bag, $12.50 shipping/3PL) at $53.50 contribution margin and a 1.87 break-even ROAS — margin more than doubles and required efficiency actually drops, letting you operate at worse ROAS at double the money.
Raise perceived gift value by selling the gift item standalone — list the bag at $60 and present the offer as $160 discounted to $100, a 40% saving rather than 'free bag'.

Layer the biggest customer objection into the higher-AOV tier, not the base: if research says buyers fear low towel quality, add a lifetime guarantee on the two-towel offer so the extra spend earns the reassurance.
caveats: The mechanic collapses if nobody wants the gift — the source stresses the offer must be convincing and grounded in real customer research, not just cheap to produce.

Add-ons like prize pools or unrelated freebies fail when the target demographic does not care; a lifetime guarantee is worthless in categories like creatine gummies where the product is simply consumed.

cards.title: Set threshold offers on the peaks of a binomial AOV distribution
cards.summary: When AOV is bimodal, set offers against each peak rather than the average or you give margin away to people who already qualify.
cards.use_when: Setting free-shipping thresholds, spend-and-get tiers or threshold unlocks when order values cluster around more than one point.
steps: Plot the distribution of order values across all customers rather than looking at the single AOV figure the platform reports.

Identify whether the distribution is binomial — two peaks, common in fashion and wide-SKU ranges where customers assemble arbitrary carts, and often shaped by an existing offer structure such as buying one or three units.

Test the failure mode with an average-based threshold: if AOV is $100 and you set free shipping at $110, customers already above $110 get free shipping for nothing (margin lost), customers clustered at $70 will never double their order, and only the thin band around $110 changes behaviour.
Instead set one offer against each peak and aim to shift both upward, using different mechanics for each peak rather than one threshold for the whole base.
Stack mechanics across peaks — for example a gift-with-purchase to lift one peak and a different mechanic for the second.
caveats: The source's figure that only about 10% of customers sit near an average-set threshold is illustrative of his example, not a general benchmark.
Binomial distributions are more common in some categories than others; verify with your own order data before assuming two peaks.

cards.title: Flat discounting: when it is appropriate and the four guardrails
cards.summary: Reserve flat discounts for high-margin SKUs or slow-moving stock, model AOV and required ROAS first, and run them only one to two times a year.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to run a straight percentage-off promotion at all, and how to keep it from becoming a brand position.
steps: Restrict flat discounting to two situations: a few SKUs with exceptionally high gross margin, or grade-C inventory that is not moving and needs converting back to cash.
Model AOV lift from previous discount periods and how they moved UPT, so you discount to the level that maximises AOV and contribution profit rather than guessing.
Model the target ROAS required at the new discount threshold and judge whether it is achievable on the platforms.
Run it rarely — the source's guardrail is one to two times per year — to preserve brand equity and price perception.
Judge the strategy by its purpose: turning stock into cash, not rescuing top-line revenue. Brands that must discount to hit a revenue figure will always have worse margins and cash flow.
caveats: The source states most businesses fall into the always-discounting trap, but presents this as a diagnosis, not an inevitable outcome.
The one-to-two-times-per-year figure is the presenter's recommendation, not a tested threshold.

cards.title: Calculate upsell and cross-sell value as incremental contribution profit
cards.summary: Optimise upsells on take rate × AOV lift × gross margin, not on any one of those variables alone.
cards.use_when: Choosing between candidate upsell or cross-sell offers, or justifying an upsell's effect on allowable CAC.
steps: Use the formula: incremental contribution profit per order = take rate % × upsell AOV lift × gross margin %.

Worked example: 10% take rate × $50 item × 50% gross margin = $2.50 incremental contribution profit per order. It looks small, but the order is already locked in and payment already captured, so it is essentially free incremental profit.

Compare candidates on the combined result, not individually. In the source's example a low-margin upsell had 20% take rate, $40 AOV lift and 30% margin ($1.60), while a high-margin upsell had 10% take rate, $30 AOV lift and 60% margin ($1.80) — the better-margin option with half the take rate won.
Feed the result back into acquisition: an extra $2 on $20 contribution profit per order is over 10%, which can raise allowable CAC by $2 and fund faster scaling.
caveats: The example numbers are illustrative; your own take rates and margins determine which candidate wins.
The source explicitly warns that pushing the highest-margin product as the upsell is a common mistake because fit and congruence drive take rate.

cards.title: Place upsells by friction: in-cart, checkout or post-purchase
cards.summary: Match the upsell's type and expected take rate to the friction of its position, with low-friction add-ons at checkout and one-click products post-purchase.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to place an upsell or cross-sell in the cart and checkout flow and what to offer at each stage.
steps: In cart: medium friction because the buyer is still deciding, so upsells can reduce purchase likelihood and take rate, which typically runs 5–15%. Use threshold unlocks, the progress bar, samples or a complimentary product when a threshold is hit.

At checkout: friction is higher than in-cart — the buyer has already committed to the order and price, so take rates decline. Avoid selling another full product; sell a low-friction add-on instead. Shipping protection at $4.99 converts around 30% in the source's experience and is effectively 100% margin because refunds are rare and usually covered by the carrier, adding roughly $1–2 gross profit per order.
Post-purchase: near-zero friction because payment is already captured; set it up as a one-click add charged to the card instantly. Take rates can reach 35–40% in the source's experience.
Apply the upsell rules: one offer per slot, relevancy over price, high-margin SKUs, easy to understand, and measured by gross margin lift rather than take rate alone.
Anchor high-value upsells and down-sells post-purchase rather than trying to load value at checkout.
caveats: Chaining multiple post-purchase offers is possible but the source notes it becomes annoying to consumers.
Take-rate figures are the presenter's observed ranges, not benchmarks guaranteed for every store.
The upside rule set is attributed to the source as his operating heuristics.

cards.title: Differentiate exit-intent and abandoned-flow offers by funnel stage
cards.summary: Match generosity to commitment: be generous to browsers, restrained for cart abandoners, and avoid margin giveaways at checkout.
cards.use_when: Designing abandoned-cart and exit-intent sequences and deciding how much to give each segment.
steps: Split exit intent into three stages by commitment: browsing, item added to basket, and reached checkout.
Browsing exits show no purchase commitment and sit nearer product aware than most aware — be generous here, give a real reason to return and attach urgency.
Basket abandoners have shown intent and may simply need one to two days; offer something small rather than giving away margin.

Checkout abandoners are closest to purchase and often just hit friction — do not discount. Use risk reversal or free shipping instead, and be sceptical about giving away margin when they will likely convert within two to three days.
Remember pop-up exit-intent modals are optional: the source dislikes them as gimmicky and prefers email-based abandoned flows for the same job.
caveats: Attributed as the presenter's opinion on offer logic and his aversion to exit-intent popups; not a tested causal result.
Stage definitions and treatment recommendations are qualitative; the source gives no conversion benchmarks for these flows.

cards.title: Value arbitrage: designing offers that feel like a steal while staying profitable
cards.summary: Consumers judge offers by the perceived gap between business COGS and what they receive, so the brand's job is to make the exchange feel lopsided in the buyer's favour while capturing spend above cost.
cards.use_when: Crafting the value mechanic of an offer, especially when a discount alone would destroy margin.
steps: Frame the buyer's view: value equals the perceived gap between the cost of goods to the business and what the buyer receives, which is why a blanket 50–60% off reads as 'they cannot be making money, so I am getting the arbitrage'.
Frame the business view as the inverse: get people to spend as much as possible above COGS while making them believe they are paying near COGS.

Use owned or partner assets to create real, deliverable value at near-zero cost — a brand that owns software can include licensing the buyer values but that costs almost nothing to deliver, making the offer genuinely good for both parties.
Layer the value mechanic with risk reversal and urgency rather than relying on the discount slot alone.
Watch perceived price anchoring: heavy flat discounting teaches customers to wait and permanently compresses the margin you planned for at launch.
caveats: This is the presenter's framing of how consumers think, offered as the best way to conceptualise the problem rather than a validated model.
The source acknowledges he does not know the compliance position on his own repackaged examples, so category-specific claims need regulatory review.

input.source_name: How 8 and 9 Figure Brands Build Offers Without Discounting.docx

cards.title: Offer vs discount: the five levers of an ecommerce offer
cards.summary: An offer is product positioning, price architecture, value mechanic, risk reversal and urgency — discount is only one option within price architecture.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing whether a brand has an ad problem, an offer problem or a discounting problem before launching new creative or a new site
steps: Define an offer as five components: (1) product positioning — what problem this solves for whom and why now; (2) price architecture — percentage off, threshold offer, units-per-transaction (UPT) structure, bundle; (3) value mechanic — free shipping, free gift, BOGO, samples, second-order tier, subscription unlock; (4) risk reversal — returns, guarantee, trial, sample-only purchase; (5) urgency — drop, seasonality, stock window.
Recognise that a discount only occupies the price-architecture slot. The other four levers can carry the offer alone, so a brand does not have to discount to have a distinct offer.

Use the value-perception mechanic deliberately: consumers judge an offer by the perceived gap between what they think the product costs the business and what they receive, so 50–60% off feels like arbitrage even when the brand is profitable; the business's goal is the inverse — capture as much spend above COGS as possible while the buyer believes they are paying near cost.
Look for offers that are genuinely good for both sides: a brand that owns a software product can bundle free licensing at near-zero delivery cost while the consumer sees real savings.
Keep the entire funnel congruent — ad, landing page, checkout and email must state the same offer, and expired promotions must not remain visible anywhere.
caveats: Rotating a new weekly promo for a 52-week calendar trains customers to wait for discounts; the source treats that pattern as a mistake, not a strategy.
Discounting permanently re-anchors perceived price, so heavy flat discounting compresses margin structurally, not just in the promo window.

cards.title: Hierarchy of influences on DTC performance
cards.summary: Budget and account structure are the lowest-leverage levers; creative, offer, brand and product drive the largest performance deltas.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest scarce time when performance is flat and teams default to reshuffling budgets and campaign structure
steps: Rank the levers from least to most powerful for creating a purchase decision: budget (fuel — more spend sells more, but only if everything else works), account structure (can retarget the same people or push the wrong products), creative (how people hear about you), offer (what they get and why now), brand (why they buy from you rather than a competitor), product (why they buy at all, dominant at bottom-funnel and repeat purchase).
Note the trade-off: higher levers create bigger deltas but are harder and slower to change, which is exactly why most teams keep fiddling with budget and account structure.
When a brand believes it has an ad problem, check the offer first; when it believes it has an offer problem, check whether the real issue is habitual discounting.
Treat budget and structure as prerequisites to fix, not as the place to hunt for inflection.
caveats: Attributed framework from the presenter; the ranking is his opinion about where leverage sits, not a measured law.
A high-level brand or product advantage does not excuse broken account structure — the lower levers can still sink an otherwise strong offer.

cards.title: Model a discount's true economics before running it
cards.summary: Waterfall price, UPT, COGS, gross margin, break-even ROAS and target CPA to see the efficiency a discount actually requires.
cards.use_when: Pressure-testing a proposed percentage-off sale or any price-architecture change against profit, not just top-line revenue
steps: Baseline the full-price unit: at $100 AOV and $40 all-in COGS (including shipping, fulfilment and transaction fees), gross margin is $60 (60%), break-even ROAS = 1 / 0.60 = 1.67, and at 6x target ROAS the target CPA = 100 / 6 = $16.67, leaving $43.33 contribution profit per order. Do this for every product.
Model the discount per unit, not per order: a 25% discount drops price per unit to $75.
Account for UPT rising during sales — in the worked example UPT went from 1.0 to 1.63, so AOV actually rose to about $122.
Compute COGS against the pre-discount retail value, not the discounted AOV: $162 retail × 40% = $65 COGS, leaving $57 gross margin (22% lower than baseline).

Recalculate: break-even ROAS rises to 2.22; holding the same contribution profit requires a CAC of about $13.67 (AOV $122 / $13.67 ≈ 8.97 target ROAS) — roughly a 50% efficiency improvement over the 6x baseline.

Ask whether that efficiency lift is realistic for this brand before launching. The source has seen luxury brands that never discount model 70–80% efficiency lifts, and saturated always-discounting brands model only about 5%.
caveats: The example assumes COGS covers all variable costs and is a simplified illustration, not a benchmark.
Efficiency lift during a sale is brand-specific; it depends on how rarely the brand discounts and how saturated the market already is with its discounting.

cards.title: Build an evergreen offer stack that lowers required efficiency
cards.summary: Layering a 90-day supply, subscription-locked lifetime discount, app access and a mystery gift cut the required ROAS from 6x to 2.9x in the worked example.
cards.use_when: Designing a non-discount-led acquisition offer that a brand can run year-round instead of rotating promos
steps: Stack components rather than discounting: buy a 90-day supply, get 25% off; free app access with daily meal plans; a free mystery gift; and a 25% discount for life while the customer stays on subscription (double the usual 10%).
Tie the offer to a required action — the buyer only gets the deal if they tick the subscription box — and put urgency behind the lifetime rate.

Model the margin: COGS at 40% of the $253 retail value is $101, but multi-unit shipping is cheaper than unit cost baked into price ($36 charged vs $17 actual for three units), pulling true delivery cost to about $82 and gross margin to $108.
Compare to the full-price baseline: holding the same contribution profit per order needs a CAC of about $65, so 190 / 65 ≈ 2.9x ROAS instead of 6x.
Keep the mystery gift out of the COGS model if it is $0–3 (sample packs, cheap drink bottles on large POs, or another brand's product supplied for co-marketing).

Note the retention upside: subscription-locked offers should drive materially more repeat purchase, which can justify even more aggressive acquisition spend — the source suggests roughly double the repeat purchasing versus a plain discount, though this is his expectation, not a guarantee.
caveats: The claim that this offer doubles repeat purchase is the presenter's projection for that hypothetical brand, not a measured result.
Do not stack value indefinitely — complexity hurts; the source warns that 'simple scales' when it comes to offers.

cards.title: Audit and iterate an offer after 90–120 days live
cards.summary: Survey customers on which offer components actually drove purchase, then cut or fix components that add complexity or damage retention.
cards.use_when: After an evergreen or heavily stacked offer has run a full quarter and you need evidence on what to keep
steps: Let the offer run 90–120 days before judging its components.
Survey buyers to establish which additions — mystery gift, app access, discount tier — convinced them to purchase.
Remove components nobody cares about and test whether conversion changes without them; the source's example was a mystery gift that may have zero persuasive value.

Investigate back-end effects of front-end winners: if an app or bonus drove acquisition but customers found it useless, it can lower brand perception and hurt retention revenue, so change the deliverable or remove it.
Iterate on this cycle to simultaneously raise first-purchase profit, lower CAC and improve retention, rather than treating acquisition and retention as separate problems.
caveats: Survey responses are self-reported and may not perfectly predict behaviour without an A/B test.
Removing a component can be tested, but the source does not specify a required sample size or test duration.

cards.title: Discount rate versus contribution profit: small discounts can lose money
cards.summary: Plotting contribution profit against discount rate shows small discounts often subtract margin with no UPT uplift, and required target ROAS rises exponentially near the profit-maximising point.
cards.use_when: Choosing the headline discount percentage for a sale or deciding whether a discount is viable at all
steps: Graph discount rate (x-axis) against contribution profit per order (y-axis) using your own historical flat-discount periods.
Expect a decline at low discounts: 5–10% is not convincing enough to lift UPT, so unit price compresses with no offset and contribution profit falls.
Find the inflection where customers begin to care and UPT rises; contribution profit is a function of both average unit retail (which falls with discount) and UPT (which rises).
Locate the discount rate at which contribution profit per order is maximised — for the source's illustrated brand that was 20% — and headline that percentage rather than defaulting to 25% or more.

Separately model required target ROAS: it rises exponentially as discounting increases because margin compresses to your profit target much faster than it compresses to zero. The worked illustration put something like a 15% discount at roughly 8x required ROAS and a 25% discount at roughly 20x, which can make deep discounting outright inapplicable.
Keep UPT and efficiency data from past promos consistent enough to make this modelling possible; messy historical discounting makes it unreliable.
caveats: Both break-even and target ROAS curves need your own UPT history; generic benchmarks will mislead.
Past 30–40% discounting the source considers the offer generally not worth it regardless of UPT uplift.

cards.title: Product repositioning: turn one SKU into many offers
cards.summary: Reposition one hero SKU into multiple personas, problems and mechanisms to unlock offers you could not otherwise build.
cards.use_when: You have a single hero SKU or narrow range and cannot construct bundles, thresholds or persona-specific offers
steps: List the distinct personas, problems and mechanisms the same product can serve. The source's example is a daily greens gummy repositioned into gut health for bloating, GLP1 support, fibre for digestion, hair health, cognition and focus, and a business-professional multivitamin — with many more tested in the account.
Build dedicated landing pages and offers around only the highest-performing angles, tailoring product title and positioning to each while leaving the SKU unchanged.

Attach costless partner value to an angle where it fits: for a GLP1-support angle, partner with a GLP1 provider for 25% off, or ask for a clip on future purchases so the offer can be revenue-positive.

Use clinical timelines as offer structure: if hair-health results are only measurable after 90–120 days, headline that requirement and add a free extra 30 days — delivered as one discounted unit on the second 90-day billing rather than extra units in the first order — to preserve first-order margin.
Note that contribution-margin impact of repositioning is nil or positive, and it works best applied to one hero SKU.
caveats: Persona repositioning can raise regulatory or compliance risk depending on claims and category — the source flags his GLP1 and hair-health examples as ideas, not approved copy.
Without repositioning, most offers collapse into broad generic promotions that fail to cut through to a specific audience.

cards.title: Bundle mechanics: protect margin and promote cheaper
cards.summary: Bundles raise UPT and create shipping/fulfilment economies of scale while protecting contribution margin if the economics are modelled.
cards.use_when: You sell multiple SKUs or a consumable you can package multiple times and want a discount-shaped offer without margin erosion
steps: Understand what a bundle changes: UPT rises necessarily, COGS efficiency comes from shipping and fulfilment rather than unit cost, and contribution margin should improve if the bundle is structured correctly.
Choose it for multi-SKU brands, or for consumables where the same SKU can be sold repeatedly — the source's example is buy two board games and get 25% off.
In the worked 90-day example, bundling cut true delivery cost from the $36 baked into price to $17, illustrating where the scale gain comes from.
Use bundles as the simple, familiar offer they are — they protect contribution margin, but the source considers them the least creative option and says teams can do much more with the same margin.
caveats: Single-SKU, non-consumable brands cannot use this mechanic.
The source notes that interviews asking candidates to define a good offer usually return 'high discount' or 'bundle', implying bundles are the obvious answer, not a sophisticated one.

cards.title: Gift-with-purchase: nearly double contribution margin at lower break-even ROAS
cards.summary: A low-cost gift that forces a second unit can double contribution margin while slightly lowering the required break-even ROAS.
cards.use_when: You have a cheap secondary SKU or accessory that pairs naturally and you want to push UPT without discounting price
steps: Model the base case (one $50 beach towel, $15 COGS, $8.50 shipping/3PL) at $26.50 contribution margin and a 1.89 break-even ROAS.

Model the offer (buy two for $100, free $4 bag, $12.50 shipping/3PL) at $53.50 contribution margin and a 1.87 break-even ROAS — margin more than doubles and required efficiency actually drops, letting you operate at worse ROAS at double the money.
Raise perceived gift value by selling the gift item standalone — list the bag at $60 and present the offer as $160 discounted to $100, a 40% saving rather than 'free bag'.

Layer the biggest customer objection into the higher-AOV tier, not the base: if research says buyers fear low towel quality, add a lifetime guarantee on the two-towel offer so the extra spend earns the reassurance.
caveats: The mechanic collapses if nobody wants the gift — the source stresses that the offer has to be convincing, grounded in real customer research, not just cheap to produce.

Add-ons like prize pools or unrelated freebies fail when the target demographic does not care; a lifetime guarantee is worthless in categories like creatine gummies where the product is simply consumed.

cards.title: Set threshold offers on the peaks of a binomial AOV distribution
cards.summary: When AOV is bimodal, set offers against each peak rather than the average, or you give margin away to people who already qualify.
cards.use_when: You are setting free-shipping thresholds, spend-and-get tiers or threshold unlocks and your order values cluster around more than one point
steps: Plot the distribution of order values across all customers rather than looking at the single AOV figure Shopify reports.

Identify whether the distribution is binomial — two peaks, common in fashion and wide-SKU ranges where customers assemble arbitrary carts, and often shaped by an existing offer structure such as buying one or three units.

Test the failure mode with an average-based threshold: if AOV is $100 and you set free shipping at $110, customers already above $110 get free shipping for nothing (margin lost), customers clustered at $70 will never double their order, and only the thin band around $110 changes behaviour.
Instead set one offer against each peak and aim to shift both upward, using different mechanics for each peak rather than one threshold for the whole base.
Stack mechanics across peaks — for example a gift-with-purchase to lift one peak and a different mechanic for the second.
caveats: The source's figure that only about 10% of customers sit near an average-set threshold is illustrative of his example, not a general benchmark.
Binomial distributions are more common in some categories than others; verify with your own order data before assuming two peaks.

cards.title: Flat discounting: when it is appropriate and the four guardrails
cards.summary: Reserve flat discounts for high-margin SKUs or slow-moving stock, model AOV and required ROAS first, and run them only one to two times a year.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to run a straight percentage-off promotion at all, and how to keep it from becoming a brand position
steps: Restrict flat discounting to two situations: a few SKUs with exceptionally high gross margin, or grade-C inventory that is not moving and needs converting back to cash.
Model AOV lift from previous discount periods and how they moved UPT, so you discount to the level that maximises AOV and contribution profit rather than guessing.
Model the target ROAS required at the new discount threshold and judge whether it is achievable on the platforms.
Run it rarely — the source's guardrail is one to two times per year — to preserve brand equity and price perception.
Judge the strategy by its purpose: turning stock into cash, not rescuing top-line revenue. Brands that must discount to hit a revenue figure will always have worse margins and cash flow.
caveats: The source states most businesses fall into the always-discounting trap, but presents this as a diagnosis, not an inevitable outcome.
The one-to-two-times-per-year figure is the presenter's recommendation, not a tested threshold.

cards.title: Calculate upsell and cross-sell value as incremental contribution profit
cards.summary: Optimise upsells on take rate × AOV lift × gross margin, not on any one of those variables alone.
cards.use_when: Choosing between candidate upsell or cross-sell offers, or justifying an upsell's effect on allowable CAC
steps: Use the formula: incremental contribution profit per order = take rate % × upsell AOV lift × gross margin %.

Worked example: 10% take rate × $50 item × 50% gross margin = $2.50 incremental contribution profit per order. It looks small, but the order is already locked in and payment already captured, so it is essentially free incremental profit.

Compare candidates on the combined result, not individually. The source's example: a low-margin upsell had 20% take rate, $40 AOV lift and 30% margin ($1.60), while a high-margin upsell had 10% take rate, $30 AOV lift and 60% margin ($1.80) — the better-margin option with half the take rate won.
Feed the result back into acquisition: an extra $2 on a $20 contribution profit per order is over 10%, which can raise allowable CAC by $2 and fund faster scaling.
caveats: The example numbers are illustrative; your own take rates and margins determine which candidate wins.
The source explicitly warns that pushing the highest-margin product as the upsell is a common mistake because fit and congruence drive take rate.

cards.title: Place upsells by friction: in-cart, checkout or post-purchase
cards.summary: Match the upsell's type and expected take rate to the friction of its position, with low-friction add-ons at checkout and one-click products post-purchase.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to place an upsell or cross-sell and what to offer at each stage
steps: In cart: medium friction because the buyer is still deciding, so upsells can reduce purchase likelihood and take rate, which typically runs 5–15%. Use threshold unlocks, the progress bar, samples or a complimentary product when a threshold is hit.

At checkout: friction is higher than in-cart — the buyer has already committed to the order and price, so take rates decline. Avoid selling another full product; sell a low-friction add-on instead. Shipping protection at $4.99 converts around 30% in the source's experience and is effectively 100% margin because refunds are rare and usually covered by the carrier, adding roughly $1–2 gross profit per order.
Post-purchase: near-zero friction because payment is already captured; set it up as a one-click add charged to the card instantly. Take rates can reach 35–40% in the source's experience.
Apply the upsell rules: one offer per slot, relevancy over price, high-margin SKUs, easy to understand, and measured by gross margin lift rather than take rate alone.
Anchor high-value upsells post-purchase and down-sell there, rather than trying to load value at checkout.
caveats: Chaining multiple post-purchase offers is possible but the source notes it becomes annoying to consumers.
Take-rate figures are the presenter's observed ranges, not benchmarks guaranteed for every store.
The rule set for upsells is attributed to the source as his operating heuristics.

cards.title: Differentiate exit-intent and abandoned-flow offers by funnel stage
cards.summary: Match generosity to commitment: be generous to browsers, restrained for cart abandoners, and avoid margin giveaways at checkout.
cards.use_when: Designing abandoned-cart and exit-intent sequences and deciding how much to give each segment
steps: Split exit intent into three stages by commitment: browsing, item added to basket, and reached checkout.
Browsing exits show no purchase commitment and sit nearer product aware than most aware — be generous here, give a real reason to return and attach urgency.
Basket abandoners have shown intent and may simply need one to two days; offer something small rather than giving away margin.

Checkout abandoners are closest to purchase and often just hit friction — do not discount. Use risk reversal or free shipping instead, and be sceptical about giving away margin when they will likely convert within two to three days.
Remember pop-up exit-intent modals are optional: the source dislikes them as gimmicky and prefers email-based abandoned flows for the same job.
caveats: Attributed as the presenter's opinion on offer logic and his aversion to exit-intent popups; not a tested causal result.
Stage definitions and treatment recommendations are qualitative; the source gives no conversion benchmarks for these flows.

cards.title: Value arbitrage: designing offers that feel like a steal while staying profitable
cards.summary: Consumers judge offers by the perceived gap between business COGS and what they receive, so the brand's job is to make the exchange feel lopsided in the buyer's favour while capturing spend above cost.
cards.use_when: Crafting the value mechanic of an offer, especially when a discount alone would destroy margin
steps: Frame the buyer's view: value equals the perceived gap between cost of goods to the business and what the buyer receives, which is why a blank 50–60% off reads as 'they cannot be making money, so I am getting the arbitrage'.
Frame the business view as the inverse: get people to spend as much as possible above COGS while making them believe they are paying near COGS.

Use owned or partner assets to create real, deliverable value at near-zero cost — a brand that owns software can include licensing the buyer values but that costs almost nothing to deliver, making the offer genuinely good for both parties.
Layer the value mechanic with risk reversal and urgency rather than relying on the discount slot alone.
Watch perceived price anchoring: heavy flat discounting teaches customers to wait and permanently compresses the margin you planned for at launch.
caveats: This is the presenter's framing of how consumers think, offered as the best way to conceptualise the problem rather than a validated model.
The source acknowledges he does not know the compliance position on his own repackaged examples, so category-specific claims need regulatory review.
